catalog_quote: ... Sebei are long or short. In addition to these two phonemic degrees of length, there are also extra-long vowels, which are non-phonemic. These occur optionally in noun forms with the thematic suffix (see Section 2.3) ... three degrees of length: long, "half-long," and short. The first two of these are assigned to the long "Chroneme," "half-long" being explained as "due to shift in stress." Since stress does not appear to be phonemic, but seems rather an effect of length plus high tone, this is presumably what Tucker and Bryan intend to convey by that statement. This assumption is supported by some of the words written with a "half-long" symbol: the Kipsigis stem for "hand" is written e:(y) (long) in isolation, e. ("half-long") when the "Secondary" suffix -- including a long vowel plus high tone -- is added (e-u:t) ... This process of length dissimilation is especially prevalent among nouns with a non-final suffix containing a long vowel and also among nouns with disyllabic stems. Although Tucker and Bryan state the qualification that in Sebei ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sebei (Kupsabiny) is a tone language (three level tones in Montgomery's analysis; five tones incl. contours in Kawachi 2015/2016) with contrastive vowel length; stress is not phonemic -- perceived prominence is a by-product of a long vowel carrying high tone, so there is no positional word-stress rule. Rottland 1982 says the same for Kalenjin generally: no phonemic stress, phonetic prominence always on non-low-toned syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Montgomery's remark is made while reinterpreting Tucker & Bryan's 'half-long' vowels ('shift in stress') as length dissimilation before a suffix with long vowel + high tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of nouns/verbs in citation and suffixed forms; statement obtained via verbatim Google Books snippet chain (dissertation has no preview), so surrounding context beyond the quoted sentences was not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Montgomery 1966 and O'Brien & Cuypers 1975 describe 'Sebei' = Kupsabiny/Kupsapiny of Sebei (Kapchorwa) District, Uganda = kups1238; Kawachi treats Kenyan Sabaot (saba1262-type variety) as a mutually intelligible dialect of the same language but his data are Ugandan Kupsapiny. Rottland 1982 sec. 5.1.3.2 is a statement about Kalenjin as a whole (his own data include Sapiny), not Kupsabiny-specific.

tone_statements.quote: Kupsapiiny distinguishes two cases – the nominative case and the absolute (object) case – with tone. The absolute case is functionally unmarked in that forms in this grammatical case occur in a wider range of environments than those in the nominative case. [...] [fn.1] Tone is distinctive in this language, though the writing system only employs a colon right before the beginning of a common noun (not of a proper noun or a pronoun) as used as the subject of a verb other than miitē ‘exist’. For the purpose of the present study, only segmental transcriptions are sufficient, with the result that tones are not represented.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Tone distinctive; grammatical tone marks nominative vs absolute case; no inventory given in this paper (Kawachi's earlier papers give 3-5 tones).

tone.quote: Kupsapiny distinguishes two cases, nominative and absolute (i.e. the case used for the grammatical object), by means of tone. It is difficult to determine which tone pattern is marked or unmarked, but because the absolute case has a wider range of uses than the nominative case, the case-marking system of this language can be regarded as marked nominative (Dixon 1994; König 2006, 2008). ... There are also verb stems that do not take a subject person suffix, but change tone patterns depending on the person.
